The mean value theorem 1.85 says more: for every piece there is a point \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) at which this is not an approximation but an exact equality,

\[u(x_{\mathrm{i}}) - u(x_{\mathrm{i}-1}) = u'(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\]

(equation (1.32)). The sum of the right sides is a Riemann sum of the strain \(u'\), and the sum of the left sides is exactly the elongation of the bar. The elongation of the bar therefore lies between the lower and the upper sum of the strain for every partition, and by lemma 3.50 it is its integral (figure 3.156). At the top of the figure is the graph of the function \(G\), which plays the part of the displacement \(u\), below it the graph of its derivative \(f\), which plays the part of the strain \(u'\), both above the \(t\) axis. The chords of the graph of \(G\) on the three pieces lie on the increments of \(G\), and the tangents at the points \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) are parallel to them, as the mean value theorem says. The height of the rectangle on a piece is \(f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\), and its area \(f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the increment of \(G\) on that piece. This argument holds for every function with a continuous derivative. Let us state it precisely.

From history

In 1599 Edward Wright published a table that, for navigation with Mercator's map, gave the length of an arc of a meridian. He computed it by successively adding the secants (sekans) of successive angles, that is, the reciprocals of their cosines (CAJORI, PDF p. 205). Around 1645 Henry Bond noticed by inspection that this is a table of logarithms of tangents (CAJORI, PDF p. 205). A sum of values of one function thus gave values of another. Newton, by his own account, conceived in 1665 and 1666 the method of fluxions (section 1.3.3) and applied it to the areas of curves. He treated the area under a curve as a quantity growing in proportion to the length of the ordinate, that is, the vertical segment from the axis to the curve (CAJORI, PDF p. 208). This is exactly the statement that the rate at which the area grows equals the value of the function. In 1668 James Gregory proved Bond's observation (CAJORI, PDF p. 205-206). In 1669 Newton placed a tract on his method in the hands of his teacher Isaac Barrow (CAJORI, PDF p. 208), and in 1670 Barrow gave his own proof as well (CAJORI, PDF p. 205-206).

In a manuscript of 1673 Leibniz noticed that the inverse problem of tangents, which asks for a curve whose tangents are prescribed, leads to finding areas under curves (CAJORI, PDF p. 223). He used a small triangle along the curve that Barrow had already used and that Leibniz, in his own words, took from Pascal (CAJORI, PDF p. 223). When he introduced the sign for a sum on 29 October 1675 (section 3.5.3), he added that a sum raises the dimension, since the sum of lines \(l\) is a region of area \(y\,a\), so the opposite calculus, the calculus of differences, must lower it (CAJORI, PDF p. 223-224). In 1676 Newton wrote in a letter, in which he hid his method in an anagram, that from an equation between changing quantities one is to find the fluxions, and conversely (CAJORI, PDF p. 228-229).

Let us return to figure 3.156, where the areas of the rectangles under the derivative \(f\) give the change of the function \(G\). Sum and difference are inverse operations, which this section states exactly in theorem 3.55 with the integral and the derivative.

Theorem 3.55 Fundamental theorem of calculus (osnovni izrek analize)
  1. Let \(G\) be a function that is continuous on a closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\), and let \(f\) be a function, continuous on \([a, b]\), for which \(G'(x) = f(x)\) for every \(x \in (a, b)\). Then
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b) - G(a) . \tag{3.55}\]
  2. Let \(f\) be a continuous function on a closed interval \([a, b]\), and let \(G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for \(x \in [a, b]\). Then \(G\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), differentiable at every point \(x \in [a, b]\), at the endpoints \(a\) and \(b\) with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), and \(G'(x) = f(x)\).
Proof

We must show both items. The first follows from the mean value theorem on every piece of a partition, the second from the bounds of the integral over a short interval.

1. The integral of a derivative.

  1. Let \(D = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}\}\) be any partition of \([a, b]\).
  2. On the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\), \(G\) is continuous and differentiable at every point of the open interval \((x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}})\). Here the assumption that \(G\) is continuous on the closed interval enters: without it we may not use the mean value theorem, and figure 3.162 shows what happens then. By the mean value theorem 1.85 there is a point \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) with \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} < \xi_{\mathrm{i}} < x_{\mathrm{i}}\) at which the tangent is parallel to the chord, and
    \[G(x_{\mathrm{i}}) - G(x_{\mathrm{i}-1}) = G'(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} = f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
  3. We add over \(i\) from \(1\) to \(n\). On the left are the increments of the function \(G\) on the pieces, stacked one on another. This is a telescoping sum, in which all the values in between cancel:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^n \big(G(x_{\mathrm{i}}) - G(x_{\mathrm{i}-1})\big) = G(x_{\mathrm{n}}) - G(x_0) = G(b) - G(a) .\]
  4. On the right is the Riemann sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^n f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\), the total area of the rectangles. Since \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a lower and \(M_{\mathrm{i}}\) an upper bound of the values on the piece, \(m_{\mathrm{i}} \le f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) \le M_{\mathrm{i}}\). We multiply by the positive length \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and add, which gives \(s(f, D) \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^n f(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} \le S(f, D)\). By step 3 therefore \(s(f, D) \le G(b) - G(a) \le S(f, D)\).
  5. The partition \(D\) was arbitrary, so the number \(G(b) - G(a)\) lies between all the lower and all the upper sums. The function \(f\) is continuous, so by theorem 3.53 it is integrable, and by lemma 3.50, item 2, the integral is the only such number. So \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b) - G(a)\).

2. The derivative of an integral.

  1. The function \(f\) above the \(t\) axis is continuous on \([a, b]\), so by lemma 1.73 it is bounded. There are therefore numbers \(m\) and \(M_0\) with \(m \le f(t) \le M_0\) for every \(t \in [a, b]\). For \(M\) we take the largest of the numbers \(|m|\), \(|M_0|\) and \(1\). Then \(M > 0\) and \(-M \le f(t) \le M\) for every \(t \in [a, b]\): the graph lies in the band between the horizontal lines \(-M\) and \(M\). The number \(1\) is among them so that \(M > 0\) even for \(f = 0\), since we divide by \(M\) in step 4.
  2. For \(a \le x < y \le b\), \(G(y) - G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^y f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), in figure 3.157 the blue strip between \(x\) and \(y\). For \(x = a\) this is the definition of the number \(G(y)\), since \(G(a) = 0\) by the convention of definition 3.49. For \(x > a\) it follows from additivity (lemma 3.54, item 2) on the interval \([a, y]\) with the point \(x\) in between.
  3. By the bounds (lemma 3.54, item 3) on the interval \([x, y]\), the area of the strip lies between the areas of the rectangles of width \(y - x\) with the heights \(-M\) and \(M\), the lower one below the axis, which counts as negative, and the upper one above it. So \(-M\,(y - x) \le G(y) - G(x) \le M\,(y - x)\) and \(|G(y) - G(x)| \le M\,|y - x|\). The inequality does not change if we swap \(x\) and \(y\), and for \(x = y\) both sides are zero. So it holds for any two points of the interval \([a, b]\).
  4. Let \(c \in [a, b]\) and \(\eta > 0\). We take \(\delta = \eta/M\). For \(x \in [a, b]\) with \(|x - c| < \delta\) step 3 gives \(|G(x) - G(c)| \le M\,|x - c| < \eta\). By step 3 the graph of the function \(G\) above the \(x\) axis lies between the lines with the slopes \(M\) and \(-M\) through the point \((c, G(c))\), so for \(|x - c| < \delta\) it stays in the rectangle of height \(2\eta\). The function \(G\) is therefore continuous at every point of the interval \([a, b]\) (definition 1.59).
  5. Now let \(x \in [a, b]\). For \(r\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(x - a\) and \(b - x\) when \(x \in (a, b)\), and the number \(b - a\) when \(x = a\) or \(x = b\). The derivative is the slope of the tangent to the graph of \(G\), so by the definition of the derivative 1.9 we must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) with \(\delta \le r\) such that
    \[\Big|\frac{G(x + h) - G(x)}{h} - f(x)\Big| < \eta\]
    for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) for which \(x + h\) lies in \([a, b]\). For \(x \in (a, b)\) these are, by the choice of the number \(r\), all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) (definition 1.5), since the distance \(r\) on both sides of the point \(x\) does not reach past the endpoints. For \(x = a\) these are the \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\), which is the condition for the limit from the right (definition 1.8), and for \(x = b\) the \(h\) with \(-\delta < h < 0\), which is the condition for the limit from the left. The other side of the point \(x\) lies there outside the interval, where \(G\) is not defined.
  6. We choose \(\eta > 0\). The function \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), so there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(t) - f(x)| < \eta/2\) for \(t \in [a, b]\) with \(|t - x| < \delta_1\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(r\).
  7. Let \(x < b\) and \(0 < h < \delta\). Then \(x + h < x + r \le b\), so \(x + h\) lies in \([a, b]\). By step 2, \(G(x + h) - G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^{x+h} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\). For \(t \in [x, x + h]\) we have \(|t - x| \le h < \delta_1\), so \(f(x) - \eta/2 < f(t) < f(x) + \eta/2\): the graph above the piece \([x, x + h]\) lies between two horizontal lines. Here the continuity of the function \(f\) at the point \(x\) enters. Where \(f\) has a jump and \(\eta\) is smaller than the jump, the graph does not fit into such a band on at least one side of the jump, for any \(h\). In figure 3.162, right, this is to the left of the point \(\tfrac12\), where \(f = 0\), while the value \(f(\tfrac12)\) is \(1\). By the bounds on an interval of length \(h\) the area of the strip lies between the areas of the rectangles of width \(h\) with the heights of these two lines,
    \[\big(f(x) - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\big)\,h \le G(x + h) - G(x) \le \big(f(x) + \tfrac{\eta}{2}\big)\,h .\]
  8. We divide by the positive number \(h\), the width of the strip, and subtract \(f(x)\) from all sides. We get \(-\eta/2 \le (G(x + h) - G(x))/h - f(x) \le \eta/2\), so the difference is at most \(\eta/2 < \eta\) in absolute value.
  9. Let \(x > a\) and \(-\delta < h < 0\). Then \(x + h > x - r \ge a\), so \(x + h\) lies in \([a, b]\). By step 2 now \(G(x) - G(x + h) = \int_{\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{h}}^{x} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), over an interval of length \(-h > 0\). As in step 7, where the graph lies between the two horizontal lines, \(\big(f(x) - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\big)(-h) \le G(x) - G(x + h) \le \big(f(x) + \tfrac{\eta}{2}\big)(-h)\). We divide by the positive number \(-h\). Since \((G(x) - G(x + h))/(-h) = (G(x + h) - G(x))/h\), we get the same estimate as in step 8.
  10. We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily. For \(x \in (a, b)\) steps 8 and 9 hold for all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), so the limit of the difference quotient, the slope of the tangent, equals \(f(x)\) (definition 1.5). For \(x = a\) step 8 holds for all \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\), so \(f(a)\) is the limit from the right (definition 1.8). For \(x = b\) step 9 holds for all \(h\) with \(-\delta < h < 0\), so \(f(b)\) is the limit from the left. In all three cases therefore \(G'(x) = f(x)\) by the definition of the derivative 1.9.

Source: LEBL1 Thm. 5.3.1 (PDF pp. 200-201) and Thm. 5.3.3 (PDF p. 202), which takes the derivative at the endpoints of the interval as one-sided. In item 1 LEBL1 asks only that \(f\) be integrable instead of continuous. We ask for continuity, which we will always have and which gives integrability by theorem 3.53.

The first item says that we compute the integral of a function \(f\) without sums if we know a function \(G\) whose derivative is \(f\). Books call such a function an antiderivative (primitivna funkcija). The second item says that every continuous function has one, namely \(G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\). Integration and differentiation are thus inverse procedures. The derivative of the integral up to \(x\) gives back the function \(f\), and the integral of a derivative gives the difference of the values at the endpoints. Figure 3.159 shows why the second item holds. On the left is the graph of a continuous function \(f\) above the \(t\) axis and the blue area \(G(x)\) from \(a\) to \(x\). When \(x\) grows by a small \(h\), the area under the graph grows by a narrow strip of width \(h\), which is approximately \(f(x)\) high. On the right is the graph of the function \(G\) above the \(t\) axis, and at the point \(x\) the tangent, which rises over a step \(h\) by \(f(x)\,h\). The change of the area divided by \(h\) is therefore approximately \(f(x)\), and step 7 of the proof wrote this approximation down exactly with the horizontal lines \(f(x) \pm \eta/2\) above and below the top of the strip.

Let us first apply the theorem to the force that pulls the bar. The function \(G(e) = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere. By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82), \((e^2)' = 2e\) and \(G'(e) = \tfrac12 k \cdot 2e = k\,e\), which is the force \(F(e)\). By item 1,

\[\int_0^{\Delta L} k\,e\,\mathrm{d}e = G(\Delta L) - G(0) = \tfrac12 k\,\Delta L^2 - 0 = 32{,}48\ \text{J} .\]

We obtained the result of section 3.5.3 in one line. In figure 3.160 it is the area of the triangle under the line of the force, above the axis of the elongation \(e\). The second item adds a physical picture. The work that the force does up to the elongation \(e\) is, by item 1 on the interval \([0, e]\), equal to \(\int_0^e k\,t\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\), and by item 2 its derivative with respect to the elongation is the force \(k\,e\). The force thus says how fast the work grows with the elongation. At the final force 10 kN the next tenth of a millimetre of elongation adds a narrow strip to the triangle, which the figure enlarges on the right. The strip is \(0{,}1\) mm wide and at its left edge 10 kN high. The rectangle of this width and height is \(10\,000\ \text{N} \cdot 0{,}0001\ \text{m} = 1\) J of work. Exactly the work is \(1{,}008\) J, because the force still grows a little over this distance, to \(10{,}15\) kN, which adds the triangle with \(0{,}008\) J. The shorter the step, the smaller the share of the triangle, and this is the content of the limit in item 2. We will use this relation between work and force in chapter 4.

Now let us keep the promise of chapter 2 and compute the displacement of the hanging bar from the stress. Recall the setting. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points down from the top, and the top of the bar, held in the ceiling, does not move, \(u(0) = 0\). The stress at depth \(x\) is \(\sigma(x) = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (equation (2.5)). We get the strain by dividing the stress by Young's modulus (section 3.1),

\[\varepsilon(x) = \frac{\rho g\,(L - x)}{E} = 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad a = \frac{\rho g}{2E} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

Dividing by \(E\) is valid as long as the steel is on the straight line of the tensile test, below the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa. The stress is largest at the top, \(\rho g L = 0{,}7652\) MPa, which is 288 times less (section 3.1.10), so the assumption holds along the whole bar. A bar in which the stress at the top exceeded the yield stress would flow there, and the displacement would no longer be the one we are about to compute. The strain is the derivative of the displacement, \(u'(x) = \varepsilon(x)\) (definition 1.10). The displacement itself we do not know. We assume only that the bar has no cracks. As for all displacements in this book, let the displacement \(u\) be continuously differentiable at the interior points of the bar (definition 1.91), and in addition continuous at both ends. So \(u\) is continuous on \([0, L]\) and differentiable at the interior points. We need the continuity at the ends because item 1 of the fundamental theorem asks for a function that is continuous on a closed interval.

  1. Let \(0 < x \le L\). By item 1 of the fundamental theorem on the interval \([0, x]\), with \(G = u\) and the continuous function \(f = \varepsilon\), the displacement of the point at depth \(x\) relative to the top is the integral of the strain from \(0\) to \(x\),
    \[u(x) - u(0) = \int_0^x 2a\,(L - t)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
  2. We compute the integral, the area under the graph of the strain up to \(x\), with the same item of the theorem, this time with the function \(H(t) = a\,(2Lt - t^2)\). By the rules of differentiation \(H'(t) = 2aL - 2at = 2a\,(L - t)\), so the integral equals \(H(x) - H(0) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\).
  3. Since \(u(0) = 0\), we get \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\). At \(x = 0\) this holds too, because both sides are zero.

This is exactly the displacement that we took as given in chapter 1 (figure 3.161). The route is now closed: from the weight we get the axial force and the stress (chapter 2), from the stress with Young's modulus the strain, from the strain with the integral the displacement. The computation tells us one more thing. The strains determine the displacement only together with the displacement of one point, here the top, \(u(0) = 0\). If we added the same number to the displacements of all points, the bar would move as a rigid body, and the strains would stay the same, because a constant has derivative zero (figure 1.330, left, from chapter 1). The elongation of the whole bar is

\[u(L) - u(0) = \int_0^L 2a\,(L - t)\,\mathrm{d}t = a\,L^2 = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 100\ \text{m}^2 = 19{,}52\ \mu\text{m} .\]

In figure 3.161 the orange bar is the bar after loading, the grey dashed outline at it is the bar before loading, and the lower end moves down by the elongation \(aL^2 = 19{,}52\ \mu\)m. The point at depth \(x\) moves by \(u(x)\). On the right is the graph of the strain above the \(t\) axis. The displacement \(u(x)\) is the area under it up to \(x\), and the elongation of the whole bar is the area of the triangle under the graph of the strain, with base \(L = 10\) m and height \(2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the strain at the top, so \(\tfrac12 \cdot L \cdot 2aL = aL^2\).

Where does the theorem fail? Item 1 requires \(G\) to be continuous on \([a, b]\). In a bar with a crack at some depth, the displacement jumps there (figure 3.162, left). The bar before loading hangs from the ceiling, and after loading the lower half moves away from the upper one. The elongation of the bar is then no longer the integral of the strains, since the jump of the displacement contributes nothing to the integral of the strains. Item 2 requires a continuous function \(f\). Where \(f\) has a jump, the graph of \(G\) has a kink above the axis: left of the kink the slope is \(0\), right of it \(1\), and \(G\) has no derivative there (LEBL1, PDF p. 203).

Let us look at a bar with a crack, with numbers. On \([0, 1]\) let the function be \(G(x) = 0\) for \(x < \tfrac12\) and \(G(x) = 1\) for \(x \ge \tfrac12\): the displacement jumps by \(1\) at the crack at \(x = \tfrac12\) (the graph of \(G\) above the \(x\) axis, second from the left). Item 1 requires three things: \(G\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\), differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, 1)\), and \(G'(x) = f(x)\) at every such point for a continuous function \(f\). Let us check them.

  1. At \(x = \tfrac12\) the function \(G\) is discontinuous: the value to the left of it is \(0\) and the value at it is \(1\). The first requirement fails.
  2. Because of the same jump, \(G\) is not differentiable at \(\tfrac12\). The difference quotient \(\big(G(\tfrac12 + h) - G(\tfrac12)\big)/h\) equals \((1 - 1)/h = 0\) for \(h > 0\) and \((0 - 1)/h = -1/h\) for \(h < 0\), which grows beyond all bounds as \(h \to 0^-\). There is no limit, so the second requirement fails as well.
  3. Everywhere else \(G' = 0\), so the only possibility would be \(f = 0\), which is continuous. But \(G'(\tfrac12) = f(\tfrac12)\) cannot hold, because \(G'(\tfrac12)\) does not exist, and the third requirement fails.
  4. The calculation \(\int_0^1 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^1 0\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) is therefore not equal to \(G(1) - G(0) = 1 - 0 = 1\). The conclusion (3.55) fails.

All three requirements therefore fail at once, the third as a consequence of the second, and the jump of the displacement does not show up in any value of \(f\): the derivative is zero everywhere it exists. Continuity on the closed interval is also needed on its own. For \(G(x) = 0\) for \(0 \le x < 1\) and \(G(1) = 1\) (the third graph above the \(x\) axis), \(G\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, 1)\) with \(G' = f = 0\), it is discontinuous only at the endpoint \(1\), where it jumps by \(1\), and again \(\int_0^1 f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \ne 1 = G(1) - G(0)\).

3.5.8 Integration by parts

In chapter 4 we will integrate products of two functions, one of which is a derivative, and we will want to move the derivative onto the other function. The tool for this comes from the rule for the derivative of a product, \((f g)' = f' g + f g'\) (lemma 1.82), and from the fundamental theorem of calculus.

From history

In Paris Leibniz divided regions with ordinates into elements. Three days before the manuscript in which he first wrote the sign for a sum, on 26 October 1675, he wrote a theorem saying that the sum of the products \(x\,w\), where the \(w\) are small parts of horizontal lines and \(x\) is a changing height, equals the last \(x\) times the sum of all \(w\), reduced by the sum of the sums of \(w\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 225-226). In the three numbers of figure 3.163 the sum of the products \(x\,w\) is the columns, the sum of the sums of \(w\) is the strips above them, the last \(x\) is the height and the sum of all \(w\) is the width of the whole rectangle.

Back to Leibniz's theorem on the sum of products \(x\,w\), which we draw with areas (figure 3.163, left). We understand the sum of sums as the sum of the partial sums, and check the theorem on three numbers, where \(x\) is successively 1, 2 and 3 and \(w\) is 5, 2 and 4. Each product \(x\,w\) is the area of a column of width \(w\) and height \(x\): \(1 \cdot 5\), \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\) and \(3 \cdot 4\), together \(21\). The last \(x\) is 3 and the sum of all \(w\) is 11, the product 33 is the area of the large rectangle. The partial sums are 5 and \(5 + 2 = 7\). They are the horizontal strips above the staircase, together 12, and \(33 - 12 = 21\). The last partial sum, \(5 + 2 + 4 = 11\), is not counted, because the last column reaches the top of the large rectangle and leaves no room for a strip above it. Each strip is 1 high, as much as \(x\) grows from one column to the next. The theorem in this form therefore holds because \(x\) grows by 1. If \(x\) grew by 2, the strips would be 2 high and each partial sum would have to be subtracted twice. Each \(w\) is counted three times in the product 33, and the partial sums take away as many as needed for each to remain as many times as its \(x\) requires: \(w = 5\) is in both strips and remains once, \(w = 2\) is in one and remains twice, \(w = 4\) is in none and remains three times. The large rectangle is thus cut into the columns under the staircase and the strips above it.

The right side of figure 3.163 shows the same idea for an integral and a derivative instead of sums and differences. Instead of three pairs of numbers we have two functions, \(f\) in the role of the height \(x\) and \(g\), whose increments play the role of the widths \(w\). We put \(g\) on the horizontal axis and \(f\) on the vertical one, and as \(x\) runs from \(a\) to \(b\), the point \((g(x), f(x))\) draws a curve. A column of height \(f(x)\) and of a width equal to the increment of \(g\) over a short step has the area of about \(f(x)\,g'(x)\) times the length of the step, so the area under the curve is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,g'\). In the same way the area between the curve and the vertical axis is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f'\,g\). The two shapes together make up the large rectangle \(f(b)\,g(b)\) without the small rectangle \(f(a)\,g(a)\). That is the whole content of the corollary below. The figure holds for increasing positive functions, where all three shapes are true areas. The corollary has no such restriction, because its proof does not use it: we derive it from the product rule, which holds for any two differentiable functions.

Corollary 3.56 Integration by parts (integracija po delih)

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions that the right side of figure 3.163 draws as the curve of points \((g(x), f(x))\) and that are differentiable at every point of the closed interval \([a, b]\), at the endpoints \(a\) and \(b\) with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), and let their derivatives \(f'\) and \(g'\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). Then the area under the curve equals the large rectangle without the small one and without the area between the curve and the vertical axis, in symbols

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f(x)\,g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = f(b)\,g(b) - f(a)\,g(a) - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f'(x)\,g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{3.56}\]
Proof

We must show that the integrals on the two sides differ by the difference of the values of the product \(f g\) at the endpoints, that is, by the large rectangle without the small one.

  1. Let \(G(x) = f(x)\,g(x)\) for \(x \in [a, b]\), in figure 3.163 the area of the dashed rectangle with a corner at the point of the curve at \(x\). The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined on the open interval \((a, b)\) and differentiable at each of its points. By the rule for the derivative of a product (lemma 1.82, item 3) with \(I = (a, b)\), \(G\) is therefore differentiable at every point \(x \in (a, b)\) and \(G'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)\).
  2. The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable at every point of the interval \([a, b]\), one-sidedly at the endpoints, so they are continuous there (lemma 1.80). By corollary 1.65 on sums and products of continuous functions the product \(G\) is therefore continuous too: when the point on the curve moves only a little, the area of the dashed rectangle changes only a little.
  3. The functions \(f' g\) and \(f g'\) are continuous on \([a, b]\) as products of continuous functions (corollary 1.65), their sum is continuous too, and by step 1 this sum equals \(G'(x)\) at every point \(x \in (a, b)\). In the figure this means that the strip along the vertical axis and the strip under the curve together tell how fast the rectangle \(G\) grows.
  4. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 1, with the function \(G\) and the continuous function \(f' g + f g'\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \big(f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b) - G(a) = f(b)\,g(b) - f(a)\,g(a) .\]
    The right side is the large rectangle without the small one.
  5. By linearity (lemma 3.54, item 1) the left side is the sum of the integrals \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f' g\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f g'\). We subtract \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f' g\) on both sides and get equation (3.56).

Source: LEBL1 Exercise 5.3.5 (PDF p. 205).

Integration by parts thus moves the derivative from the function \(g\) to the function \(f\), at the price of the term \(f(b)\,g(b) - f(a)\,g(a)\), the large rectangle without the small one, which contains only values at the endpoints. The name says that we split the integral into parts: the product at the endpoints and a new integral. At the endpoints \(a\) and \(b\) the corollary asks only for a one-sided derivative, the limit of the difference quotient from one side: the band of allowed steps \(\Delta x\) reaches to one side of zero only, because the functions may not be defined outside the interval \([a, b]\) (figure 1.44). The displacement of the bar is such a function, known only from \(x = 0\) to \(x = L\). LEBL1 states the same formula, for functions that are continuously differentiable on \([a, b]\), with the derivative at an endpoint as in Def. 4.1.1 (LEBL1 Exercise 5.3.5, PDF p. 205, Def. 4.1.1, PDF p. 155). Polynomials are differentiable everywhere and meet the condition.

Let us test the formula on the hanging bar, on which we will see its meaning in chapter 4. The bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight (figure 3.66, left), the axis \(x\) points down from the top, and the top does not move. The axial force is \(N(x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\), the displacement \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\). Take \(f = N\) and \(g = u\), both polynomials. Their derivatives are \(N'(x) = -\rho g A\) and \(u'(x) = 2a\,(L - x)\). Equation (3.56) gives

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = N(L)\,u(L) - N(0)\,u(0) + \int_0^L \rho g A\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x .\]

The term at the endpoints is zero, and for two physical reasons. The lower end is free, so there is no axial force there, \(N(L) = 0\). The upper end does not move, \(u(0) = 0\). What remains is

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L \rho g A\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x .\]

On the left are the axial forces times the strains, on the right the weights of the pieces per unit length times the displacements. Let us check the equality with the fundamental theorem of calculus. On the left the integrand is \(\rho g A\,(L - x) \cdot 2a\,(L - x) = 2a\,\rho g A\,(L^2 - 2Lx + x^2)\). The function \(L^2 x - L x^2 + x^3/3\) has the derivative \(L^2 - 2Lx + x^2\), so

\[\int_0^L N(x)\,u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 2a\,\rho g A\,\Big(L^3 - L^3 + \frac{L^3}{3}\Big) = \frac23\,a\,\rho g A\,L^3 .\]

On the right the integrand is \(\rho g A\,a\,(2Lx - x^2)\). The function \(L x^2 - x^3/3\) has the derivative \(2Lx - x^2\), so

\[\int_0^L \rho g A\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \rho g A\,a\,\Big(L^3 - \frac{L^3}{3}\Big) = \frac23\,a\,\rho g A\,L^3 .\]

With \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), \(\rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m and \(L^3 = 1000\ \text{m}^3\) both sides equal \(7{,}821 \cdot 10^{-4}\) J. What this equality means we will see in chapter 4.

Why the two sides are equal is shown in figure 3.164. At the top we draw the axial force \(N\), which falls from \(\rho g A\,L = 60{,}10\) N at the top of the bar to zero at the free lower end, and the displacement \(u\), which grows from zero at the fixed top to \(a\,L^2 = 19{,}52\ \mu\text{m}\) at the bottom. Below, as on the right side of figure 3.163, we put \(u\) on the horizontal and \(N\) on the vertical axis. As \(x\) runs from the top to the bottom, the point \((u(x), N(x))\) draws a curve from a point on the vertical axis to a point on the horizontal axis. The rectangle \(N(0)\,u(0)\) from the endpoint \(x = 0\) has zero area, because at the top \(u = 0\), and so has the rectangle \(N(L)\,u(L)\) from the endpoint \(x = L\), because at the bottom \(N = 0\). A single shape under the curve remains, which we draw twice. We divide the bar into five pieces of length \(\Delta x = 2\) m. On the left we cut the shape into vertical strips: the strip at \(x\) is \(\Delta u\) wide, as much as \(u\) grows on the piece from \(x\) to \(x + \Delta x\), about \(u'(x)\,\Delta x\), and about \(N(x)\) high, so its area is about \(N(x)\,u'(x)\,\Delta x\). Towards the bottom the strips get narrower, because there the displacement grows more and more slowly. As the pieces get shorter, the sum of these areas approaches the integral \(\int_0^L N\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x\). On the right we cut the shape into horizontal strips: the strip at \(x\) is \(\rho g A\,\Delta x = 12{,}02\) N high, by which the axial force falls on the piece, and about \(u(x)\) long, so its area is about \(\rho g A\,u(x)\,\Delta x\). All horizontal strips are equally high, because the axial force falls evenly. As the pieces get shorter, the sum approaches the integral \(\int_0^L \rho g A\,u\,\mathrm{d}x\). The two integrals are therefore one and the same area, \(\tfrac23 \cdot 60{,}10\ \text{N} \cdot 19{,}52 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m} = 7{,}821 \cdot 10^{-4}\) J.

With the integral we can now compute the work done by a changing force along a straight path, when the force changes continuously, and the displacement of a bar from its strains. The next section will ask where the work goes that the machine does on the bar when it slowly stretches it.
